text.p: Kenya's Wilson Boit Kipketer, who won a dramatic battle with compatriots Moses Kiptanui and Bernard Barmasai to win his first world steeplechase title last week, was pulled along to a world record by the pair on Wednesday.

Kipketer held off Kiptanui and Barmasai in a fast last lap to clock seven minutes 59.08 seconds, shaving one tenth of a second from the previous best of 7:59.18 set by Kiptanui on the same Zurich track in August 1995.
Kiptanui, who had to settle for second place behind Kipketer at this month's world championships in Athens, finished third in 8:00.78 behind second-placed Barmasai who ran 8:00.35.
The performance at the most lucrative meeting in athletics was worth a world record bonus of $50,000 to Kipketer plus one kilo of gold.
With appearance fees the Kenyan, who is not related to the 800 metres runner Wilson Kipketer, walked away from Zurich at least $100,000 richer.

"When so many Kenyans start together in a race in this stadium, the only possibility is to expect a world record," Kiptanui said. "To me, it is a motivation and I would like to try at least once more but it's getting harder and harder."

Kipketer, who has been working hard on finishing his races strongly with specific training, added: "I didn't expect the record. I just felt good and ran. I still have a lot of respect for Moses Kiptanui."
The race was the highlight of the first major meeting since the world championships finished in Athens last Sunday.
Newly-crowned sprint champions Maurice Greene and Marion Jones were warned that they have a tough fight on her hands to stay at the top when both Americans were beaten over 100 metres.
Greene finished second behind Namibia's Frankie Fredericks who won in 9.98 seconds. Greene finished one hundreth of a second behind.

Jones failed to match the strong finish of Jamaican veteran Merlene Ottey and also had to settle for second, one hundreth of a second behind the 37-year-old Ottey who won the women's 100 in 10.96. Olympic champion Gail Devers took third in 11.06.
The meeting brought together 25 of the world champions from Athens.
Double Olympic champion Michael Johnson, who retained his 400 metres world title in Athens despite a season of injuries, had to work hard to win the 400 metres in 44.31.
After cruising through the first 200 metres, Johnson stepped up a gear in the final bend but was pushed all the way down the home straight by compatriot Tyree Washington and Uganda's Davis Kamoga.

Washington took second in 44.38 with Kamoga third in 44.43. Although the time was below his best for the season, the fans at the end of the straight greeted Johnson like a hero, chanting his name like a soccer crowd.
"It was a close race and I'm happy I was able to win," Johnson said. "My objective now is to win races. I was injured for a long time so I want to compete until the end of the season."
American world and Olympic champion Allen Johnson enhanced his position as the leading high hurdler in the world with victory in 13.13 seconds against a headwind.
American Mark Crear and Britain's Tony Jarrett took second and third in 13.14 and 13.21 respectively while Britain's world record holder Colin Jackson had to settle for fourth in 13.30.
Johnson still has the world record in his sights in the lucrative meetings around Europe in the next few weeks.
"I didn't run as well as I could. I hit many hurdles," he said. "But it's still a fast time. I have still got four races in Europe and I'm still motivated to break the world record."
